turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mrs Pillay. Sit where you're comfortable. What's been happening, in your own words?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doctor, I'm all right, truly. I slid down twice, but I didn't fall, hey, I just slid. And when I stand up the room goes funny and I get so frightened. Is it a stroke?

[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She fell, doctor, twice, properly. The second time she was on the bathroom floor and she couldn't get herself up. I stay with her, so I see it. She tells everyone she only slid.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I slid onto the mat. You did help me, well, actually, yes, the second time. My hip is a bit sore, that's all. I'm not dying, am I?

[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, I can see you're worried. I don't think this is you dying, and a stroke isn't the first thing on my mind, but we'll go through it properly. When did the dizziness start?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Last winter, or the winter before, I mix them up. It was there around Easter, or just after the long weekend, I can't pin the date.

[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The two falls were this past month, the first a Tuesday and the second Sunday morning by the toilet. She's dizzy every single time she stands, for ages. She makes it sound like nothing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every time. Sometimes. Sitting I'm not dizzy. If I hold the chair, is it still a stroke, and can I still go to church on Sunday?
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sitting steady is a good sign, and we'll come to church once I understand the tablets. Are you dizzy while you're sitting at all, any chest pain, or did you black out?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I didn't black out, I remember the mat and I remember her voice. Sitting I'm fine, the standing is the problem.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Tell me what tablets you take for the blood pressure, and anything you take for sleep.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The white one is five milligrams, I take that, and a water tablet, and the sleeping one at night. I don't skip them. Well, I don't think I skip them.

[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The white one is amlodipine and the packet is ten milligrams, not five. Enalapril ten milligrams every morning, hydrochlorothiazide twelve point five every morning, and zopiclone seven point five at bedtime so she sleeps. She's been on the blood pressure treatment for years.
[SEG0014] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry, doctor, I'll be quick. The repeat script on the file says amlodipine ten milligrams daily. And I've done the lying and standing blood pressures.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? Ag no, sister, that's not right, I take five. I break it in half most days, and sometimes the other half is still there in the morning, I think. Yoh, am I overdosing?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can't tell you if it's five or ten that actually goes in. Some mornings the half is still in the Monday slot. She gets muddled with the pill box.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll treat the dose as not settled, and you're not in trouble. Sister, read me those pressures, please.

[SEG0018] person_4 (NURSE): Lying, after five minutes, one hundred and fifty-six over ninety-two, pulse seventy-four. Standing at one minute, one hundred and twelve over seventy, pulse ninety-six. She swayed, but I kept a hand on her.

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): One hundred and twelve? That can't be, this morning the home machine said eighty-eight over fifty-something, I looked. So which number is real? Am I going to faint in the shop?
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was ninety-six over sixty on the home monitor, not eighty-eight. You had your glasses off. It was still low, and she was pale.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Home and here can both be real, and the drop from lying to standing is the bit that worries me. Any headache, or weakness down one side, when you slid?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, no weakness. My left hip is just sore where I landed. If the numbers jump around like that, do I stop all the tablets tonight, all of them?

[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There's a bruise on the left hip, purple, bigger than she'll admit. And she's more wobbly in the passage at night, especially when the load shedding hits and the light is off. I stay in the back room, so I hear her.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The bruise is small. The load shedding isn't your problem, shame, but I do get scared in the dark. Will I fall again tonight?

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see a bruise on the left hip, a few centimetres across, tender, and the skin isn't broken. Your grip is equal and your face is symmetrical, and I don't find a weak side.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's not a stroke, you're sure? What about my heart, can the heart do this?

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling it a stroke. My working impression is a postural drop in the blood pressure, very likely aggravated by the tablets. A heart rhythm problem is still possible, I can't rule that out today.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Postural, does that mean if I stand slowly I'm safe? And the sleeping tablet, is that the bad one? I need it, doctor, otherwise I'm awake all night worrying.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does take the zopiclone every night, that one I'm sure of. The amlodipine is the messy one. And she asks me ten times if she's already taken it.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to stop the zopiclone from tonight. Sleeping tablets and a postural drop are a bad mix when someone is already sliding. We'll leave the enalapril and the water tablet as they are for now.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop it completely? What if I don't sleep? Can I take half a sleeping tablet? Just now I'll be up all night and then I'll fall anyway.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not even half, no zopiclone. If you're lying awake, get up only with the passage light on, and sit on the edge of the bed before you stand. That part is on you and on your carer tonight.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): And the white tablet, the five or the ten, what do I do with that one in the morning? I don't want to take the wrong thing and collapse at the chemist.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep taking one amlodipine as the packet is printed, the ten milligram, and don't snap it, until we see the bloods. I'm not changing that one today, because we still don't know what you've actually been swallowing.
[SEG0035] person_4 (NURSE): I can take the bloods after this, doctor, if you want them today. She's had water, and she hasn't eaten since early, she said.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes please. Kidney function, sodium, and a glucose, and an ECG before she leaves. The rhythm is the thing I can't see with a blood pressure cuff.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles, I hate needles. Is the sugar one a finger prick or the arm, and do I have to take my blouse off for the ECG? There was a lady in the waiting room coughing, is that a problem for me?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bloods from the arm, and the blouse comes up a bit for the stickers, with the curtain closed. The cough next door isn't yours. We might do a scan of the head if this dizziness hasn't settled, but not today.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): If a scan happens later, should I book transport now? The nephew's bakkie is only free on Thursdays. She still wants to know about church.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't book a scan. It's only if it hasn't settled, we might, and I'll tell you at the review. Church is fine if someone walks with you and you sit, rather than stand, for the long hymns.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I slide again before I see you? Do I come back, or go to emergency, or just phone? I'm going to phone you at midnight, I'm warning you.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two weeks, here in the rooms. If you fall again, or you faint, or one side goes weak, don't wait, go to casualty. Not a midnight phone call to me, hey.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Casualty, all right. And my hip, do I need an x-ray? It could be broken and you're just looking at a bruise.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): It doesn't look broken. You walked in and the hip joint moves, so I'm not ordering an x-ray today. If the hip pain is worse rather than better in a few days, then we might x-ray it.

[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch the hip, and I'll put the zopiclone away so it isn't sitting by the bed. Do you want the old boxes brought next time, the amlodipine as well, so you can see the strength?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, bring all the boxes next visit, that helps me more than anyone's memory. Sister will do the bloods and the ECG now, and then you can go home.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Bring the boxes, stop the sleeping tablet, bloods, the ECG, back in two weeks, and if I feel funny standing I sit down. Did I miss anything? I'm still scared.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): You didn't miss it. Light on at night, someone with you at church, and we'll know more once these tests are back. Off you go with sister.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Transcript names zopiclone, not zolpidem; doctor stops zopiclone from tonight.
bad.text: zolpidem (dose=7.5 mg, frequency=at bedtime, indication=sleep, status=discontinued, reported_by=doctor)

bad.reason: Completed is supported, but nurse did not request it; she only says she has done it.
bad.text: Lying and standing blood pressure (type=other, status=completed, requested_by=nurse)

bad.reason: Doctor says a head scan might be done later if dizziness hasn't settled; CT is not specified.
bad.text: CT scan of the head (type=imaging, status=conditional, requested_by=doctor, indication=if the dizziness has not settled)

omissions.text: Medication recorded wrongly: the sleeping tablet discussed and stopped was zopiclone 7.5 mg at bedtime, not zolpidem.

Amlodipine dose/use details were not fully captured: caregiver and repeat script say amlodipine 10 mg daily, but the patient says she often breaks it in half and may effectively take 5 mg, with leftover half tablets in the pill box some mornings.
Doctor explicitly decided to leave enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide ('the water tablet') unchanged for now.
Standing blood pressure was measured at one minute after standing, after lying for five minutes.
Caregiver reported the second fall was on the bathroom floor by the toilet on a Sunday morning, and the patient could not get herself up.
The patient remembered the event ('the mat' and the caregiver's voice) when denying blackout.
Caregiver reported the patient asks repeatedly whether she has already taken the amlodipine, supporting medication confusion/adherence problems.
Home blood pressure was disputed: patient said 88 over 50-something, while caregiver corrected this to 96/60.

Doctor documented additional examination detail that the patient's face was symmetrical and grip was equal, and specifically said he did not find a weak side; the current extraction combines some of this but misses the explicit equal grip detail.
Doctor advised that if lying awake at night, the patient should get up only with the passage light on, and this responsibility is shared by the patient and carer that night.
Nurse noted the patient had had water and had not eaten since early before the planned blood tests.
ECG and blood tests were to be done that day before she left, by the nurse.
